summary: For ages 11–12: order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions on a single number line (leftmost = least), and use =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ to compare values, including negatives and mixed representations. The core principle is that POSITION on the line — not sign, digit count, or denominator size — is the single rule that orders every kind of number, and that equal values (e.g. 0.75 and 3/4) sit at the same point, so neither < nor > holds between them; = is the precise relation, and ≤ and ≥ are also true. The primary activity is a hands-on positional sort of mixed-form cards with a common-form conversion check; supporting activities consolidate symbol conventions, interrogate wrong orderings, and read statements in context.
misconceptions: Ordering negatives by magnitude (−5 placed as greater than −2)
Comparing fractions and decimals by surface features instead of converting to a common form
Confusing < and > direction (the 'alligator eats the bigger' heuristic misapplied)
Treating ≤/≥ as identical to </> and missing the equality case
Assuming a longer decimal or larger denominator is automatically larger/smaller

activities.title: Drop mixed-form numbers onto one number line and choose the symbol between neighbours
steps: Take a set of mixed cards — 0.75, 3/4, −0.8, −0.75, 7/10, −2, −1.5, 1/2 — and place each at its correct position on a shared number line.
Use a 'show as decimal' conversion (e.g. 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75) to check cross-form values before placing them.
Notice that 0.75 and 3/4 land on the IDENTICAL point and coincide there.
Between each adjacent pair of placed cards, select a symbol from =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ and justify the choice.
Confirm that between the two coincident cards the strict symbols < and > (and ≠) are false; = is the most precise choice, and the inclusive ≤ and ≥ are also true because they allow equality.
Deliberately test the surprise case: see that −0.8 sits LEFT of −0.75, so −0.8 is smaller, even though 0.8 > 0.75 for positives — defeating the 'bigger magnitude wins' instinct for negatives.
activities.insight: Position on the number line (left = less) is a single rule that orders integers, decimals, fractions, positives and negatives uniformly; equal values coincide, so < and > cannot hold between them, while = (and the inclusive ≤, ≥) are true.

activities.title: Consolidate the symbol conventions with true/false and ordering checks
steps: Judge true/false statements such as '−5 < −2' and explain the reasoning from position.
Match order statements to the correct symbol from =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥.
Order a mixed-form set smallest to largest as a sequence.
Write a single statement using ≤ that is true for all of 2, 2.0, 4/2.
activities.insight: Order statements and symbol conventions (including strict vs inclusive) can be applied fluently once positional ordering is understood.

activities.title: Interrogate and repair a wrong ordering in discussion or context
steps: Examine a given ordering that mis-ranks negatives (e.g. −5 placed to the right of −2) and explain why it is wrong, referring to position.
Read comparison statements aloud in context, e.g. '−3 > −7 means −3°C is warmer / further right than −7°C'.
Decide when ≤ would be used instead of < between two values, and say why.
State an inference about relative size from a placement, e.g. which of −2 and −1.5 is smaller and why.
activities.insight: Articulating WHY an ordering is right or wrong — in words and in real contexts like temperature — reinforces positional reasoning and distinguishes strict from inclusive comparison.

checkQuestion: Give a mixed set: −2, 0.75, 3/4, −1.5, 1/2. Say: 'Place these on a number line and order them smallest to largest. Then put the right symbol between 0.75 and 3/4, and between −1.5 and −2.'
